title: Jensen Huang wasn't mentioned in latest talks with China, Bessent says
description: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaking on CNBC's Squawk Box on Nov. 13, 2026.CNBCFormer Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not mentioned in the Trump admi
body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaking on CNBC's Squawk Box on Nov. 13, 2026.CNBCFormer Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not mentioned in the Trump administration's latest talks with China, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" Friday. "No," Bessent said without elaborating when asked if Huang, a close ally of President Donald Trump facing allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy, had come up in those talks.Bessent also suggested that U.S. policy allowing the sale of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China remains unchanged following the discussions. "We've already agreed that the that H200s are the threshold level of chips that could be sold to the Chinese, and, you know, that continues as planned," Bessent said. "I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy," he added after CNBC's Sara Eisen noted that Nvidia said it had stopped selling H200s to China.Bessent's appearance came after Trump's return from a tour through Asia that saw him meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.The meeting was historic as the first time the leaders of the three countries had met without other countries' counterparts. But the trilateral summit appeared to yield few deliverables on any number of the most pressing global issues related to the countries, including the Ukraine and Iran wars or the ongoing AI race.There was a "robust discussion" between Trump and Xi on trade policy and AI, Bessent told CNBC.They "agreed that humans should always be involved in any military decisions that SI makes, and the SI should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions," he said, abbreviating the term "super intelligence," Trump's attempted rebrand of AI. This is developing news. Please check back for updates.

schema.headline: Jensen Huang wasn't mentioned in latest talks with China, Bessent says

title: Forget Anthropic: In Europe, the IPO hype is about a blue lagoon
description: People bathing in The Blue Lagoon, a geothermal bath resort in the south of Iceland.Getty ImagesWhile investors are fixated on Anthropic's blockbuster
body: People bathing in The Blue Lagoon, a geothermal bath resort in the south of Iceland.Getty ImagesWhile investors are fixated on Anthropic's blockbuster stock market debut, a very different IPO is making waves in Europe: Iceland's Blue Lagoon, the operator of one of the world's most famous geothermal spas.Blue Lagoon Corp. raised roughly 14.3 billion Icelandic kronur ($110 million) through the offering, valuing the Icelandic geothermal spa operator at about $787 million, according to the company's investor presentation.The Blue Lagoon traces its origins to 1992, when Blue Lagoon Ltd. was founded to study the water in the Blue Lagoon, an open-air pool of warm, milky-blue water set in a black lava field in southwestern Iceland. It grew into a business spanning a spa, hotels and skincare made with ingredients from the lagoon.Shares will trade under the ticker "BLUE" on one of Europe's smallest stock exchanges, Nasdaq Iceland Main Market, part of the Nasdaq Nordic group, which also operates exchanges in Sweden, Denmark and Finland.'Wellness is the new luxury'"Wellness is the new luxury, and we know that the wellness economy is growing faster than the economy as a whole, so we have tailwind from that," CEO Sigríður Margrét Oddsdóttir told CNBC on Thursday."Now is the right time for us to list," she added. "We are a company that thinks long-term, we have a clear vision for the next decade, and being publicly listed gives investors the opportunity to participate in our journey."The company's operations are centered on Iceland's Reykjanes Peninsula, where, as well as the Blue Lagoon geothermal spa, it runs the Silica Hotel, the Retreat luxury hotel and spa, and the Michelin-starred Moss restaurant. It also operates the Kerlingarfjöll Highland Base and Hrauneyjar properties in Iceland's highlands, and sells Blue Lagoon-branded skincare products internationally.The 34-year-old company has averaged 11% annual revenue growth over the past decade, and next year is expected to be a record, with revenue growing by more than half, Oddsdóttir said.The company plans to use the raised capital to fund expanding its existing properties, acquiring businesses, and developing new destinations.In total, nearly 4,000 subscriptions were received in the initial public offering, worth about 15.3 billion kronur, about 7% more than the total size of the offering, the company said, citing strong demand from smaller investors, including retail investors.Iceland's relatively small stock market had just 27 companies on its main exchange at the end of 2025, according to Nasdaq. The market is dominated by banks, seafood companies and other domestically focused firms.Iceland's growing wellness industryThe global wellness industry reached $7.5 trillion in 2025, up 8.9% from the previous year, according to the Global Wellness Institute. Spending on thermal and mineral springs grew 10.4% over the same period, with the institute forecasting annual growth of nearly 10% for the sector through 2030.Tourism accounted for nearly 9% of Iceland's GDP in 2025, and is growing, according to Statistics Iceland. The country welcomed around 2.3 million international visitors that year, with the U.S. as its largest source market.

schema.headline: Forget Anthropic: In Europe, the IPO hype is about a blue lagoon

title: The bull market has a new problem. The 'smart money' is selling
description: Anthropic billboards are displayed in Times Square as shares begin trading after their IPO on November 19, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago
body: Anthropic billboards are displayed in Times Square as shares begin trading after their IPO on November 19, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago | Getty ImagesCompanies have shifted from buying back shares to issuing them, adding to the supply that the four-year-old bull market must absorb. "No matter how you measure it, U.S. corporations have changed their behavior over the past two years, switching from repurchasing in 2024 to issuing today," Acadian Asset Management portfolio manager  Owen Lamont wrote in a letter to investors this month. "The question you should be asking is: Why is the smart money selling?" As of late last week, net new issuance of shares equaled 3.1% of total market capitalization, according to a recent Acadian analysis. While net issuance remains below the peaks during the tech bubble and the covid bubble, the analysis shows that the era of repurchases has ended and an era of equity issuance has begun. And more supply came to the market this week with Anthropic's blockbuster IPO. The offering drew strong enthusiasm initially with the frontier AI laboratory selling shares in its IPO at $83 each, above the expected range and raising $81 billion. But the stock is falling on Friday and taking the broader stock market with it.Some investors for years have cited the shrinking stock market as a reason why share prices can keep increasing. As companies repurchased stock, it shrunk the number of shares available for trading and so it helped boost prices. There was more money chasing fewer shares. Not to mention, it had the effect of boosting earnings per share by lowering the denominator in that ratio. Now that trend has reversed with increased supply acting as a potential headwind on the bull market.A 2000 paper by Malcolm Baker and Jeffrey Wurgler found that when companies issued more equity over debt, low market returns followed, suggesting that managers timed the market when issuing securities. The Baker-Wurgler equity share, which measures equity issuance as a share of total stock and bond issuance, peaked at about 18% in 2021. It has risen in recent months but remains below that peak, Lamont wrote.The Federal Reserve data show a similar trend in the year-over-year change in trailing 12-month gross stock and bond issuance. Debt gross issuance rose first in 2020, followed by equity issuance in 2021. More recently, debt issuance began climbing in 2024, followed by a surge in equity issuance in 2026. Recent deals show companies tapping equity markets in different ways.Oracle filed to sell $20 billion in stock through an at-the-market program and issued another $10 billion in common shares in November. In October, Meta priced a $25 billion common-stock offering and $12.5 billion in mandatory convertible preferred shares. Alphabet announced an $84.8 billion equity raise in June to help fund its AI infrastructure buildout. SpaceX raised $85.7 billion in its June IPO after underwriters exercised their overallotment."Before 2026, firms were net repurchasers of equity, consistent with the idea that they viewed their shares as undervalued. Today, for whatever reason, firms are issuing equity on net," Lamont wrote.The investor said he cannot rule out that we are in an AI bubble now.

schema.headline: The bull market has a new problem. The 'smart money' is selling

title: White House replaces cyber director Sean Cairncross amid widespread tech outages
description: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, with Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies set to serve as acting director after a week
body: White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, with Pentagon CIO Kirsten Davies set to serve as acting director after a week of high-profile U.S. technology outages.The role, which advises the president on cybersecurity and coordinates U.S. cyber policy across federal agencies, has been handed to Davies, the Pentagon's chief information officer, on an interim basis. A permanent national cyber director must first be nominated by the president and then confirmed by the Senate.Axios first reported Cairncross' exit, citing two White House officials who said President Donald Trump's chief of staff, Stephen Miller, pushed for his departure. The White House declined to comment. However, a source familiar with the White House's thinking told CNBC that the President fully supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position because he lacked the strong cyber credentials to perform the job. Davies has the credentials to excel in the position and has been Senate-confirmed, the person added. The Office of the National Cyber Director did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. United States National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross attends an event with U.S. President Donald Trump in the Oval Office of the White House on June 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. Andrew Harnik | Getty ImagesIt comes after a series of technology outages, including a nationwide aviation ground stop, a worldwide Microsoft Outlook outage and a reported blackout of the National Security Agency's classified communications network.The White House has insisted that there are no indications of a coordinated cyberattack, state-sponsored activity or malign actor behind recent tech outages. Davies addressed her responsibilities in the new position and thanked Miller and Trump for their confidence late Thursday."Our nation stands in the crossroad of analog, digital, and quantum technologies, our American way of living increasingly interconnected. Our opportunity is to dominate the cyber landscape for generations to come … but only if we modernize and drive resilience into the foundations our great nation runs on," she wrote on X.Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both congratulated Davies on her appointment.

schema.headline: White House replaces cyber director Sean Cairncross amid widespread tech outages

title: Gap names new Athleta CEO, lowers full-year guidance
description: A Gap store stands in Times Square on March 5, 2026, in New York City.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesGap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will b
body: A Gap store stands in Times Square on March 5, 2026, in New York City.Spencer Platt | Getty ImagesGap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that."I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement.The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month. "Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode."Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential. Third-quarter earningsGap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount. Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%. Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share. Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season."We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said. Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:Earnings per share: 82 cents adjusted vs. 78 cents expectedRevenue: $4.01 billion vs. $4.02 billion expectedFor the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior. Brand salesA shopper walks past an Athleta store at Fashion Valley, an upscale shopping mall in San Diego, California.Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesAt Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing. The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales. "Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said. The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2. Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country."We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth."

schema.headline: Gap names new Athleta CEO, lowers full-year guidance

title: AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure
description: watch nowShares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report al
body: watch nowShares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."CNBC did not independently verify this information.Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconAMD, 1-dayThe allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia. "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

schema.headline: AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure

title: Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’
description: watch nowCathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.Wood's firm, whic
body: watch nowCathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm."We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday."We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together. Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble."Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

schema.headline: Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’

title: U.K.-India trade deal faces a stiff test over Scotch whisky import taxes
description: MUMBAI, MAHARASHTRA, INDIA - 2025/10/09: A man talking on his mobile phone walks near the poster of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi welcoming his
body: MUMBAI, MAHARASHTRA, INDIA - 2025/10/09: A man talking on his mobile phone walks near the poster of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi welcoming his counterpart, Prime Minister of United Kingdom, Keir Starmer at a street corner in Mumbai. Sopa Images | Lightrocket | Getty ImagesWithin months of taking effect, the India-U.K. trade deal is facing an early test, as New Delhi resists extending preferential tariffs to bulk Scotch whisky imports.Duty on bulk Scotch whisky imports was expected to be slashed to 75% then gradually to 40% over 10 years as per the trade agreement. However, a Reuters report Thursday said that India now plans to levy a 162.5% duty on these imports, higher than the 150% in place before the trade deal.While India's commerce ministry did not respond to CNBC's request for comments, experts said that authorities in India classify bulk Scotch as a raw material and claim the preferential tariffs accorded in the deal apply only to imported bottled Scotch.Amid the confusion over tax rates, thousands of liters of bulk Scotch in more than 80 shipping containers belonging to Pernod, Diageo and Bacardi are stuck at Indian ports, according to Reuters."Ministers are urgently working with the Government of India to resolve this issue to ensure UK businesses can export under the tariffs agreed in the trade deal," a U.K. government spokesperson told CNBC.Distillers in India use bulk Scotch in their own locally blended whisky brands. As a result, Indian tax authorities are classifying bulk Scotch as "compound alcoholic preparations" which do not qualify for the preferential rate, said Sohrab Bararia, partner and leader of global trade at Grant Thornton Bharat. Meanwhile, distillers argue that "genuine Scotch whisky" does not cease to be whisky merely because it is imported in bulk containers or used later for blending and bottling in India, Bararia said.After three years, including 14 rounds of rigorous negotiations, India and the U.K. finalized the deal last year, which is expected to boost bilateral trade by 25.5 billion pounds ($34 billion) per year by 2040. Officials from Diageo and Chivas Brothers had cheered the trade deal and underscored its importance for Scotch and Scotland. "India is the world's largest whisky market by volume, so Scotch was always going to be one of the biggest prizes for the UK in this deal," said Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft. Instead of simply exporting bottled whisky, bulk scotch exports offer British producers long-term ties with companies in India, deepening their stake in the South Asian country's domestic alcoholic beverage industry, Bhattacharya said.Market accessIn the global spirits markets, while the U.S., Europe, and China are facing volume contraction, ageing populations, and shifting social habits, nearly 100 million new consumers will be of legal drinking age in India over the next five years, Indian brokerage HDFC Institutional Research said in a report in September.The alcoholic beverage market in India is dominated by Indian-made foreign liquors (IMFL), as per the report. IMFL refers to alcoholic beverages produced in India by combining local spirits often with imported malts and flavorings.Greater access to bulk Scotch stocks at competitive prices helps Indian distilleries to improve blending quality for premium whisky products while maintaining cost efficiency, experts said. However, the latest dispute poses a major threat to these operations.The lack of preferential tariffs on bulk Scotch could have "substantial" financial implications for importers, Parth Shah, partner at Deloitte India, told CNBC. "This could particularly affect Indian manufacturers who have invested in domestic blending and bottling operations using imported bulk Scotch whisky," he added.Diageo-owned United Spirits, Pernod Ricard and Indian firms Allied Blenders and Radico Khaitan own and market some of the popular whisky brands in India. Companies and industry bodies, the International Spirits and Wine Association and Confederation of Indian Alcoholic Beverage Companies, did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. A spokesperson for one of the whisky makers told CNBC that industry bodies were in talks with the commerce ministry to "represent adherence to the India-UK FTA." The person did not wish to be identified as they fear it could lead to a potential backlash from regulators."The lesson for the EU and other partners negotiating with India is that securing a headline tariff reduction is only half the battle," Bhattacharya of Maplecroft Verisk said, adding that partners need to pay close attention to whether "concessions translate into actual market access."

schema.headline: U.K.-India trade deal faces a stiff test over Scotch whisky import taxes

title: U.S.-China trade, Taiwan and tech tensions remain unresolved as Trump returns from Asia
description: US President Donald Trump and China's president Xi Jinping pose for a photo during a bilateral meeting in Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pac
body: US President Donald Trump and China's president Xi Jinping pose for a photo during a bilateral meeting in Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. Doug Mills | Afp | Getty ImagesSHENZHEN, China — Even as Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders gathered for high-profile photos at the summit's close, key issues from Nvidia to Taiwan remained unaddressed. "The intrigue is around not what was said, but what remains unresolved," said Gary Dvorchak, managing director at Blueshirt. "Taiwan remains a major source of strategic uncertainty. North Korea was notably absent from the trilateral nuclear declaration," he said. "Southeast Asia, which is increasingly central to global manufacturing and investment, was overshadowed by major-power diplomacy."President Donald Trump did not meet with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un, despite speculation. Taiwan, one of the 21 member economies of APEC, sent Acer Group founder and honorary chairman Stan Shih to Shenzhen. But the self-governed island, which Beijing claims is part of its territory, did not feature in any significant way during the event. Taiwan is set to hold key elections for Taipei mayor and other posts on Nov. 28.Instead, the highlight of this week's APEC summit in Shenzhen was a trilateral meeting Thursday between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The three leaders, meeting together for the first time, reaffirmed interests in reducing nuclear risks and plans to increase oil production."The optics are impressive, but there's not much happening," Ian Bremmer, president and founder of Eurasia Group, said Friday of the trilateral on CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia."Resolving the years-long Ukraine war would require involvement from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies, Bremmer said.Little on tariffs, or Elon MuskAhead of the trilateral, Trump and Xi also held their third bilateral summit of the year. Xi greeted Trump at the airport late Wednesday, reciprocating the hospitality shown in September when the Chinese leader visited Washington.But little was shared publicly on whether the two countries agreed to reduce tariffs further, allow rare earths to keep flowing beyond a January deadline, or address tech competition.Recent reports tying Jensen Huang to an alleged Chinese spy led to the executive's resignation as Nvidia CEO. It also raised questions in Congress about the effectiveness of U.S. efforts to restrict China's access to advanced chips used to train artificial intelligence.Trump indicated to Fox News that Nvidia came up briefly in his talks with Xi. U.S. officials last week said Trump did not plan to raise the matter, while noting Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk would accompany the U.S. president.No other executive was named. Other American business leaders, including Visa CEO Ryan McInerney, who also chairs the U.S.-China Business Council, joined the APEC CEO Summit and was seen at a welcome banquet Wednesday evening.In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin, China's President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump pose for photos as they arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong province, on November 19, 2026.  Vyacheslav Prokofyev | Afp | Getty ImagesHowever, Musk did not appear with Trump at major APEC-related events. CNBC was present for the opening portions of a banquet Wednesday and the Economic Leaders' Meeting Thursday and did not see Musk.In fact, Musk flew to Shanghai Thursday morning to visit Tesla's factory there, a company executive said on Chinese social media. Musk also showed up in a social media video with Ren Hongbin, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade.Musk addressed Wednesday's DealBook Summit in New York via video conference, having previously said on X that he would be joining from China.Tesla and the White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment."We still don't have a durable resolution of the U.S.-China trade dispute," Dvorchak said, adding: "Business needs certainty, not just ceremony."U.S. builds interests in Asia outside ChinaTrump visited Shenzhen after briefly traveling to the Philippines on Tuesday for a meeting with the leaders of Australia, India and Japan as part of the Quad grouping happening on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit. Trump also met the prime minister of Thailand, Anutin Charnvirakul.Topics of discussion included U.S. cooperation with the region, trade and critical minerals, U.S. Ambassador to ASEAN Kevin Kim told reporters Wednesday. He declined to comment on whether China's influence in the region was addressed.Kim emphasized it was the second year in a row that Trump visited Southeast Asia, and noted the region "will be at the heart of SI [artificial intelligence] going forward," making it important that American technology is "getting into the right hands" through a regulatory framework the president is building. Speaking to reporters a day later in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also highlighted the ASEAN and Quad events over APEC. "The major outcome of this diplomatic week was the Quad Summit," she said, noting via official English translation how the four leaders expressed "strong opposition to the unilateral approach to change the status quo by force or coercion ... [as well as] arbitrary export control." Takaichi, the first Japanese leader in seven years to visit China, received a cool reception upon her arrival in Shenzhen for the APEC meeting. China's President Xi Jinping (C), U.S. President Donald Trump (R) and Russia's President Vladimir Putin (L) take part in a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. (Photo by Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)Mandel Ngan | Afp | Getty ImagesTensions between Japan and China have escalated since Takaichi drew Beijing's ire in Nov. 2025 when she said that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could draw a Japanese military response.Takaichi said Thursday that Japan's position on Taiwan remained unchanged as stated in the 1972 Japan-China Communiqué.The communique said Japan "understands and respects" the People's Republic of China's position on Taiwan, but does not explicitly acknowledge Taiwan as part of the PRC.— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

schema.headline: U.S.-China trade, Taiwan and tech tensions remain unresolved as Trump returns from Asia

title: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
description: SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk," CNBC
body: SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk," CNBC has learned.Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5.It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington. The battle for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has reached new heights in 2026 as Chinese models have improved.But now Cursor plans to "explore phasing out PRC [People's Republic of China]-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk," according to a report produced by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, shared exclusively with CNBC ahead of its publication on Friday.The report, which follows a months-long investigation into the adoption of Chinese AI models into the American tech stack, said Cursor "informed the Committees" of those plans. Airbnb and DoorDash also engaged with the investigation about their use of Chinese AI models. watch nowSpaceX announced it entered into a formal agreement to buy Cursor in June; the deal was completed in August. SpaceX is developing the Grok family of models, which Cursor has been involved in training. Cursor, SpaceX and DoorDash did not respond to a CNBC request for comment. Airbnb declined to comment. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Chinese AI adoptionThe report found that cost, customization and near-frontier performance of Chinese AI models were driving adoption, with the U.S. lacking a competitive open-weight alternative at "price and performance the market demands.""Beijing is now seeking to turn those technological gains into global market share and long-term dependence," the report says. China's embassy in the U.K. did not respond to a request for comment. China's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond.It also sets out recommendations to address the issues it has identified.Those include launching a "national American open-weight initiative" that combines public computing power, shared evaluation infrastructure and "lawful access" to American frontier models for training. The report also says an order, made public in October, that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, should be built on, by prohibiting the use of "PRC-developed AI models" in federal information systems and in performance of federal contracts.Separately, Washington is also concerned about Chinese companies accessing Nvidia chips remotely, via overseas data centers, and gaining ground by using "distillation," where new models use older, more established ones to help train them. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.

schema.headline: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models

title: Bitcoin suffered identical sell-off pattern ahead of Anthropic, SpaceX IPOs — what happens next?
description: Sebastien Bozon | Afp | Getty ImagesBitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving in
body: Sebastien Bozon | Afp | Getty ImagesBitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Ether declined 25.3% in the 30 days preceding Anthropic's debut, and 28% in the same window ahead of SpaceX."Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink, told CNBC. "The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market.""Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash."While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment.Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns."[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management, a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here."The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said. "Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable."Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000.As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35.Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said."Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite.""The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin."

schema.headline: Bitcoin suffered identical sell-off pattern ahead of Anthropic, SpaceX IPOs — what happens next?

title: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
description: The logo of the Italian technology company Bending Spoons SpA is pictured on the facade of the company's headquarters on November 16, 2026 in Milan, I
body: The logo of the Italian technology company Bending Spoons SpA is pictured on the facade of the company's headquarters on November 16, 2026 in Milan, Italy.Emanuele Cremaschi | Getty ImagesTax software maker Intuit said Thursday that it has agreed to sell marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock. The deal is set to close in early 2027, according to a statement.The sale is a costly retreat for Intuit, which paid $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021 in a push beyond its core tax and accounting businesses. Five years later, the software maker is unloading the email-marketing company for less than one-third of that price after Mailchimp became a drag on its overall revenue growth.The deal is the latest instance of Bending Spoons picking up a once promising technology asset. The company bought productivity software startup Airtable in September for 10% of what it was once worth.The Bending Spoons portfolio also contains AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo, and WeTransfer. In August Intuit started running Mailchimp as a distinct operating segment. The move was meant to give investors more transparency as the company tried to manage the unit for profitability, Sandeep Aujla, Intuit's finance chief, said at a September company briefing.Also on Thursday, Intuit announced stronger-than-expected earnings and revenue for its fiscal first quarter, which ended on Oct. 31. The company reported $2.91 in adjusted earnings per share on $4.35 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $2.70 per share and $4.31 billion in revenue. While Intuit's revenue increased 12% year over year, Mailchimp revenue declined 1% to $313 million. Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $314.4 million.Management called for $22.88 to $23.12 in adjusted earnings per share for the 2027 fiscal year, with $23.081 billion to $23.365 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $23.62 in adjusted earnings per share on $23.43 billion in revenue. Intuit shares tumbled 15% in extended trading.The company said Mailchimp should produce $1.256 billion to $1.266 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, which would be down 1% to flat year over year. In August Aujla said Intuit anticipated Mailchimp's higher effective prices offsetting increased client churn. Mailchimp was founded in 2001. Rivals include Klaviyo, which went public in 2023.Berkshire Hathaway invested $600 million in Bending Spoons when the acquirer went public in July, and in October Bending Spoons said Berkshire invested another $330 million.WATCH: Intuit shares fall on guidancewatch now

schema.headline: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion

title: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
description: Mary Barra, chief executive officer of General Motors Co., center, outside the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Michael N
body: Mary Barra, chief executive officer of General Motors Co., center, outside the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, US, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesFormer General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra: "It's going to be tough."He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence, vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles."It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a big change."Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson, CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable."watch nowHis comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise."Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.Stellantis, BMW, Toyota Motor, Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.GM succession planningBarra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates."Selecting Barra as CEOWhen Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said.Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.GM Chairman and CEO Dan Akerson, left, announces he is stepping down during a town hall meeting at the GM Renaissance Center Global Headquarters in Detroit, Dec. 10, 2013. Listening are Mary Barra, the new CEO; Dan Ammann, the new president; and Mark Reuss, the new executive vice president for global product development, purchasing and supply chain.Photo by Steve Fecht for General MotorsAkerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann, an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021."Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson said. "She's done a terrific job."Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker."This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

schema.headline: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'

title: Senate passes BAAJA permitting reform bill backed by AI, energy sectors
description: An aerial view of wind turbines at the Altamont Pass wind farm on Jan. 13, 2026 in Livermore, Calif.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesThe Senate on Thursd
body: An aerial view of wind turbines at the Altamont Pass wind farm on Jan. 13, 2026 in Livermore, Calif.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesThe Senate on Thursday passed a long-sought bill to ease the nation's environmental permitting laws and overhaul electrical transmission regulations, a crucial step toward boosting construction for the energy and technology industries.Senators voted 62-33 to pass the bill, which split Democrats just weeks after they flipped enough seats from Republicans in the midterm elections to give them majorities in both chambers of Congress in January. The bill, known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, is projected to lower energy costs for consumers while weakening some environmental laws to speed up the permitting process. The vote offers a window into the fissures forming in the Democratic Party as it prepares to assume full control of Congress in January and tries to address the affordability crisis that catapulted it to power. More Democrats voted against the permitting measure than voted for it. Still, more than a dozen — including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. — voted to pass it over the objections of climate groups and tribes to get the bill across the finish line. "It's going to be legislation that's really going to make the biggest difference for the next 100 years, especially bringing down carbon emissions once this president is gone," Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., told reporters on Thursday before the vote. Gallego supported the measure. The bill's Senate passage is a key step to it becoming law, but it would also need to clear the House before heading to President Donald Trump's desk.Democratic supporters of the bill touted its cost benefits as a win after they ran campaigns on affordability, and pointed to a massive glut of clean energy the bill could bring onto the grid. Opponents lamented rollbacks to the nation's bedrock environmental protection laws favored by the fossil fuel industry and Republicans, and warned the measure could offer carte blanche authority to the data centers undergirding artificial intelligence. "No big, bipartisan bill is going to be perfect for everyone, but we have a real opportunity to make electricity more affordable for families. Working people can't afford to wait another few years for us to get this done," Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., the incoming chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and an author of the bill, said in a statement to CNBC. From left, R-W.Va., Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., hold a news conference on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, September 30, 2026.Bill Clark | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesHeinrich brokered the agreement with his counterpart Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, along with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., the top Democrat and Republican on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.   "Earlier this month, Americans sent a clear message: They want Congress focused on making their lives more affordable. That's precisely what this permitting reform bill will do," he said. Getting to a final vote was acrimonious. Senators amended the package in the weeks leading up to the vote to address concerns from Native American tribes, which objected to changes in their participation in permitting. "I'm not going to sit around and let these data centers scar our treasures," Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., told reporters Thursday about the push for his amendment, which would have blocked data centers from being built on public lands. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., is seen during votes in the U.S. Capitol on June 17, 2026.Tom Williams | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty ImagesClean energy and fossil energy groups both cheered the bill's passage in the Senate. As negotiated, the bill would benefit both renewables and fossil fuels. Artificial intelligence and the broader tech industry also stand to benefit — despite the bill's provision forcing hyperscalers to pay for upgrades to the grid — as power-hungry data centers demand more electricity.The American Clean Power Association, a group that represents renewables, said it was "a clean energy bill that will modernize America's energy systems and lower consumer prices."The American Petroleum Institute, which represents the oil and gas industry, called the bill a "major breakthrough on historic permitting reforms that would deliver more affordable energy for consumers, cut costly delays, and build much-needed critical infrastructure."Renewables would benefit largely from the bill's electricity transmission component, along with measures aimed at blocking Trump from cancelling already-permitted wind and solar projects. New solar and wind projects are often bottlenecked by a lack of transmission able to deliver power to the grid. Rhodium Group, an economic research firm, estimates the bill would allow an additional 17 to 249 gigawatts of clean energy to be built by 2040. Natural gas exports would rise 8% to 15% beyond a 76% to 145% rise already accounted for under current policy. Greenhouse gases would be reduced by 5 to 148 million metric tons annually in 2040. "A lot of Democrats are involved and supportive in this deal because expanding grid capacity would integrate a lot of clean energy," said Rob Gramlich, the founder and president of Grid Strategies, an energy consulting group. "Republicans are maybe less interested in that benefit, but they do care about economic growth and serving new large loads. And I think members on both sides of the aisle are pretty well aware that we're doing much less grid investment here in the U.S. compared to other countries." Gramlich added that "you can't get to 60 to 80% of our grid from renewable energy without a significant expansion of grid capacity." However, the Natural Resources Defense Council was among the opponents."The House should not pass a bill that gives President Trump a blank check to reward oil and gas companies and data center developers," the organization said in a statement. "Lawmakers should oppose this bill and try again next year to pass legislation worthy of the American people, not for the fossil fuel industry and data center companies."The bill now heads to the House, where Republican leadership is expected to attempt to pass it. Trump also supports the deal. But as in the Senate, Democrats are expected to be divided. "Democrats promised to lower bills, cut pollution, and protect ratepayers," said Rep. Scott Peters, D-Calif., a longtime champion of permitting reform. "Voters are giving us a chance to show we mean it. BAAJA does all three. We should pass it before the end of this Congress."House Natural Resources ranking member and likely incoming Chair Jared Huffman, D-Calif., meanwhile, urged Democrats to say no to the permitting bill. "Don't believe the lie that this terrible bill, exactly as drafted, is the last, best and only chance to ever do permitting reform," he said. "We can produce a better deal."

schema.headline: Senate passes BAAJA permitting reform bill backed by AI, energy sectors

title: Jensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloons
description: File: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum at the Kennedy Center in Washington, Nov. 19, 2025.Stefani Reynolds | Bloomberg |
body: File: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum at the Kennedy Center in Washington, Nov. 19, 2025.Stefani Reynolds | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe still-unraveling scandal of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs and the tech giant's potential role in its advanced semiconductor chips ending up in China present a legal minefield for Huang and Nvidia.Federal and state prosecutors and Nvidia employees may target Huang and the company in court, where some shareholders have already taken action.That's on top of a rapidly growing pile of probes by Republicans who control Congress now and Democrats who will have majorities in both the House and Senate come January."It's not going to get any better for Jensen Huang; it's going to get far worse," said Salvatore Graziano, a New York securities litigation attorney at Bernstein, Litowitz, Berger & Grossmann. His firm is looking at shareholder lawsuit opportunities against Nvidia and Huang.[Huang] "faces the Department of Justice, the Securities and Exchange Commission and private litigation," Graziano said. "The criminal exposure is very serious. The SEC could bar him from being an officer. And the potential liability [from shareholder] lawsuits can be very large."Huang's and Nvidia's legal exposure stems from three issues that led up to his shock resignation Nov. 12.There's his alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who worked for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under investigation for diverting advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules. That, in turn, has raised questions about whether Huang and Nvidia were aware of any diversions.There are Huang's two other alleged affairs with Nvidia employees.And there is the sharp drop in the company's stock price in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's share price has fallen 19% since Nov. 8, when Huang sent a company-wide apology acknowledging extramarital affairs.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia share priceHuang last week retained the law firm Paul, Weiss and its attorneys Melinda Haag and Walter Brown to represent him. Haag is a former U.S. attorney in San Francisco, and Brown is also a former federal prosecutor.Huang's spokesman at Trident, a crisis communications firm, declined to comment when asked if Haag and Brown are representing him in any potential criminal case and other questions about his legal exposure.Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Last week, Nvidia retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation into Huang allegedly being targeted by a spy, as U.S. intelligence reportedly has concluded.Read more CNBC news on NvidiaJensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloonsTrump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX amid federal contractsKress tells employees 'let's move forward' at first all-hands meeting since Huang exitPRO: Here's what every major Wall Street analyst is saying about Nvidia after its earnings reportKress tells Jim Cramer that 'customers continue to be with us'Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China access: SourcesThe civil liability Huang and Nvidia could face is underscored by a hearing Graziano, the securities attorney, attended Tuesday in U.S. District Court in San Francisco. A judge at the hearing approved a $175 million settlement from Seagate Technology Holdings to resolve a shareholder lawsuit alleging it concealed sales of hard-disk drives to Huawei in China in violation of export bans. The Seagate settlement came three years after the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security — which is investigating Megaspeed's business with Nvidia — imposed a $300 million penalty on Seagate for its sales to Huawei.Graziano said his law firm is "actively looking at securities law liability for Nvidia, Jensen Huang and other senior executives in the company given all the recent developments regarding their [potential] knowledge and facilitation of illegal chip sales to Chinese entities." One shareholder suit has been filedThere is already a pending class-action shareholder lawsuit in San Francisco federal court against Nvidia and Huang by the Rosen Law Firm, for allegedly misleading and false statements related to Megaspeed and Alice Huang. "Several hundreds of investors have contacted us and expressed an interest to join the case — investors of all walks of life, from mom and pops to investors with very large losses," Rosen attorney Phil Kim told CNBC in an email. Katie Sweeten, a former federal prosecutor in the DOJ's National Security Division, said the question of "who knew what and when, and what was [Huang's] role" is potentially the biggest risk for Nvidia and him."Now DOJ can leverage their criminal authorities," Sweeten, a partner at Scale LLP, told CNBC's Kelly Evans on "The Exchange.""They can bring grand jury subpoenas, search warrants for emails, bank accounts, personal devices, computers, things like that," Sweeten said.While it is "not illegal to, you know, sleep with a spy ... it is illegal to pass certain types of information to a counterintelligence officer," she said.Sweeten also pointed to potential export control violations, which "could be very serious."She noted the DOJ can indict a company as well as its officials if there is evidence of criminality. Export control violations carry a maximum possible criminal sentence of 20 years in prison and "really large fines," she said."You can't send the company to prison, but they can face fines, civil penalties, debarment — where you can't export items down the line," she said.One example of that came in July 2025, when the DOJ obtained a guilty plea and an agreement to pay more than $140 million from Cadence Design Systems for violating the Export Control Reform Act by unlawfully exporting semiconductor design tools to China's National University of Defense Technology, a school led by China's Central Military Commission.Congressional hearings present riskAnother potential legal risk for Huang comes from his planned appearances before Congress.Huang is scheduled to give a closed-door interview Dec. 1 to three House committees. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., wants Huang's testimony before that panel to be public, and told CNBC Tuesday he hopes to have that happen "before Christmas."Sweeten said Huang "has to be very careful" about what he says there because of the risk of being criminally charged with lying to Congress, and of saying something "that absolutely can become part of a criminal or civil investigation.""I expect Huang to take the Fifth on most questions" from Congress, Jonathan Kanter, a former assistant attorney general in the DOJ's Antitrust Division, told CNBC, meaning Huang will likely use his constitutional right against giving testimony that could be used against him in a criminal case."With a Justice Department criminal investigation into Megaspeed already underway and more investigations possible, anything he tells Congress could be used against him," Kanter said. "His lawyers are likely to advise him against taking that risk."Ben Heineman Jr., a former senior vice president and general counsel of General Electric, and a senior fellow at Harvard University, told CNBC that Nvidia's board will be scrutinized over its actions before it pushed Huang to resign.Heineman cited the board's apparent lack of succession planning and what looks like weak oversight of Huang, including relating to personal conduct such as the two alleged affairs with Nvidia employees and with an executive of an Nvidia customer."When there is a sort of reasonable suspicion, they need to investigate it, and they don't appear to have done that," Heineman said.State attorneys general may circleNvidia and Huang could face investigation from state attorneys general, including in California, where the company is headquartered.On Tuesday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta told Bloomberg Television that the situation at Nvidia with Huang is "something that we're interested in." Bonta's office later told CNBC, "We are monitoring the situation."Huang's alleged affairs with Nvidia employees also open the possibility of workplace litigation.Ari Wilkenfeld, a Washington-area employment lawyer, said a consensual relationship between a chief executive and a subordinate "is not in and of itself illegal.""The liability never comes from the existence of the relationship alone. It comes from whether it was genuinely welcome, what job benefits flowed from it, and what it did to everyone else in the building," Wilkenfeld said. "California law recognizes that so-called sexual favoritism can create a hostile environment for an entire workforce."The affair is Huang's problem," Wilkenfeld said. "What, if anything, Nvidia did once it knew is the company's problem."

schema.headline: Jensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloons
